prompt.brief: Design a multi-tenant job scheduling service that runs one-time and recurring jobs reliably, even when schedules spike, workers fail, or a dispatcher is restarted.
successSignals: Separate schedule management, due-work detection, dispatch, and execution.
Explain timing semantics, duplicate delivery, retries, time zones, and missed runs.
Use durable state and leases so dispatcher and worker failures recover safely.
Make tenant fairness, backpressure, idempotency, and operational visibility explicit.

functional: Create, update, pause, resume, and delete one-time or recurring schedules.
Run HTTP, container, or queue-backed jobs with configurable timeout and retry policy.
Support cron-like expressions, time zones, start/end windows, and misfire policy.
Expose execution history, current state, manual run, cancellation, and dead-letter replay.
Isolate tenants with quotas, concurrency limits, authorization, and audit events.
nonFunctional: Provide at-least-once execution with a clear idempotency contract; exactly-once side effects are the job owner's responsibility.
Target p99 dispatch lateness below 10 seconds for jobs within the normal capacity envelope.
Survive dispatcher, worker, queue, and storage node failures without silently losing a due job.
Keep schedule writes strongly consistent while allowing dashboards and metrics to be eventually consistent.
Apply backpressure and tenant fairness instead of allowing one customer to exhaust all workers.
scaleAssumptions: 10 million active schedules, with 100 million executions per day.
Average execution rate is about 1.2K jobs/second; peak bursts reach 10K jobs/second.
Most schedules are recurring and produce a small schedule row plus one execution record per run.
Jobs are external work: median runtime is 5 seconds, with a 15-minute maximum lease and timeout.

dataFlow.title: Create or update a schedule
dataFlow.description: The service validates timezone, cron, retry, concurrency, and tenant policy, then atomically updates schedule state and its due-time index.

dataFlow.title: Discover due schedules
dataFlow.description: Partition owners scan bounded due-time buckets, acquire leases, and fence stale dispatchers before producing execution messages.

dataFlow.title: Run with lease and idempotency
dataFlow.description: Workers claim an execution, renew its lease, use a stable run key, and record heartbeats and terminal status.

dataFlow.title: Retry or dead-letter
dataFlow.description: Transient errors are rescheduled with bounded backoff; exhausted or non-retryable failures enter a tenant-visible dead-letter queue.

dataFlow.title: Recover dispatcher gaps
dataFlow.description: A reconciler compares schedules, leases, queue messages, and executions to repair missed dispatch without creating a duplicate run.

architecture.title: Distributed job scheduler reference architecture
architecture.summary: A durable schedule store feeds a partitioned dispatcher, which claims due work and hands it to queues so execution remains reliable under retries and worker churn.

deepDives.title: Due-time indexing and dispatcher leases
points: For the multi-tenant job scheduler, each scheduled occurrence creates at most one logical execution while allowing safe attempts.
Design for the failure case where dispatcher restart, clock skew, worker loss, and retry storms must not duplicate or starve jobs; keep retries, versions, and repair state explicit.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

deepDives.title: Exactly-once run intent
points: For the multi-tenant job scheduler, each scheduled occurrence creates at most one logical execution while allowing safe attempts.
Keep this concern off unrelated request paths and partition it by the multi-tenant job scheduler access key.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

deepDives.title: Retries, fairness, and recovery
points: For the multi-tenant job scheduler, each scheduled occurrence creates at most one logical execution while allowing safe attempts.
Keep this concern off unrelated request paths and partition it by the multi-tenant job scheduler access key.
Expose freshness, version, lineage, or audit metadata so operators and clients can distinguish current, pending, and degraded state.

tradeoffs.title: Polling due indexes versus timer queues
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use a durable due-time index with partition leases and bounded polling; add timer services only when scale requires it.
tradeoffs.caution: A single timer coordinator becomes a failover bottleneck; unbounded polling burns capacity.

tradeoffs.title: At-most-once versus at-least-once execution
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use at-least-once dispatch with stable run keys and application-level idempotency.
tradeoffs.caution: At-most-once can silently lose a job during a lease or worker failure.

tradeoffs.title: Strict fairness versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Reserve tenant quotas and weighted queues while allowing controlled borrowing of idle capacity.
tradeoffs.caution: Pure global FIFO lets one noisy tenant dominate; rigid isolation wastes capacity.

commonMistakes: Computing next-run time outside the schedule write transaction.
Assuming a queue message implies a job ran exactly once.
Using leases without fencing stale dispatchers.
Leaving missed runs, timezone, and DST behavior unspecified.

followUps.question: What happens if the dispatcher crashes after claiming a schedule?
followUps.answer: The lease expires, a new owner reclaims it, and a stable occurrence/run key deduplicates any already-enqueued execution.

followUps.question: How do you handle a burst at midnight?
followUps.answer: Pre-shard due buckets, apply tenant fairness and backpressure, and let schedule freshness or misfire policy be explicit.

followUps.question: How do you prevent duplicate side effects?
followUps.answer: Pass a stable occurrence key to the job, record attempts with conditional writes, and require downstream idempotency for external effects.

rubric.description: The answer defines schedule semantics, due-time indexing, leases/fencing, idempotent execution, retries, fairness, and recovery, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure behavior.
Entities and keys make the multi-tenant job scheduler state, versions, lifecycle, and derived projections explicit.
Partitioning, queues, backpressure, cache behavior, hot-key handling, and bounded work are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded behavior, observability, and auditability protect the primary contract.
The candidate can explain the multi-tenant job scheduler consistency boundary, asynchronous work, and operational limits.
